## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a
  HyperFrames player widget that renders the project inline. Both the thumbnail
  and the preview HTML are regenerated server-side at request time.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,

 "screeningLimitations":"No systematic search is described, so the selection of studies is not reproducible. Most effect sizes are taken from earlier meta-analyses, and the review offers no new athlete data beyond its illustrative example.",

 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Rappelt L, Javanmardi S, Heinke L, Baumgart C, Freiwald J. The multifaceted nature of recovery after exercise: A need for individualization. Sports Orthop Traumatol. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.orthtr.2023.10.006",
   "abstract":"This review argues that recovery after exercise involves physical and psychological processes that vary across individuals and time spans, so group-mean evidence may not guide individual decisions. It summarises common recovery methods and their meta-analytic effects and calls for individualised, repeatedly measured approaches.",
   "tldr":"Recovery methods do not act the same way across outcomes, time points or athletes, so choose them by the sport, the time until the next session and what the individual's markers show. Repeated individual monitoring is needed to check whether a method works for a given athlete.",
   "methods":"Narrative review with no described search strategy. The authors summarise recovery definitions, the Bishop recovery time spans, a classification of recovery methods, and meta-analytic effect sizes from earlier studies (Table 1). They also present a small randomised trial comparing cold water immersion, percussive massage and passive rest after depth jumps.",
   "findings":"Table 1 reports that cryotherapy reduces delayed onset muscle soreness (trivial to large effects, 0 to 96 h) and that compression garments increase muscular strength within 24 h (small to large). BCAA reduce creatine kinase at 48 h (moderate) and creatine at 48 to 96 h (large). Protein shows small to medium strength effects. In the illustrative trial (cold water immersion n=11, percussive massage n=11, passive rest n=10), method-by-time interactions were large, especially immediately after the protocol, and individual time courses differed markedly from the group means.",
   "limitations":"No systematic search is described, and the effect sizes are taken from earlier meta-analyses with differing protocols. The illustrative trial is small and single, so it cannot establish individual responses. The authors note that the effects of cold water immersion on long-term strength adaptation remain uncertain.",
   "practicalImplications":"Choose recovery methods by sport, the time until the next session and the outcome that matters, and track individual markers such as strength, jump height and creatine kinase over repeated sessions. Do not assume a method that helps the group average will help every athlete.",
   "athleteDev":"Use the time course of each outcome to decide when to test readiness after hard training, for example jump or strength checks at 24 to 72 h, and record each athlete's response over repeated sessions.  ABSTRACT

The influence of muscle morphology and strength characteristics on sprint running performance,

especially at elite level, is unclear. Purpose: This study aimed to investigate the differences in

muscle volumes and strength between male elite sprinters, sub-elite sprinters, and untrained

controls; and assess the relationships of muscle volumes and strength with sprint performance.

Methods: Five elite sprinters (100 m seasons best [SBE100]: 10.10 ± 0.07 s), 26 sub-elite


                                                                            D
sprinters (SBE100: 10.80 ± 0.30s) and 11 untrained control participants underwent: 3T magnetic

resonance imaging scans to determine the volume of 23 individual lower limb




                            EP
muscles/compartments and 5 functional muscle groups; and isometric strength assessment of

lower body muscle groups. Results: Total lower body muscularity was distinct between the




                              TE
groups (controls < sub-elite +20% < elite +48%). The hip extensors exhibited the largest muscle

group differences/relationships (elite, +32% absolute and +15% relative [per kg] volume vs sub-

elite; explaining 31-48% of the variability in SBE100), whereas the plantarflexors showed no

differences between sprint groups. Individual muscle differences showed pronounced anatomical

specificity (elite vs sub-elite, absolute volume range +57% to -9%). Three hip muscles were

               C
consistently larger in elite vs. sub-elite (TFL, sartorius, gluteus maximus; absolute +45-57% and



  C
relative volume +25-37%), and gluteus maximus volume alone explained 34-44% of the variance

in SBE100. Isometric strength of several muscle groups was greater in both sprint groups than



A
controls, but similar for the sprint groups and not related to SBE100. Conclusions: These findings

demonstrate the pronounced inhomogeneity and anatomically specific muscularity required for

fast sprinting, and provides novel, robust evidence that greater hip extensor and gluteus maximus

volumes discriminate between elite and sub-elite sprinters and are strongly associated with

sprinting performance. Key Words: Sprinting, muscle volume, isometric strength

demonstrated very strong relationships between muscle volume and neuromuscular power of

Practical Summary and Implications
The extensive differences in muscle morphology between elite and sub-elite sprinters and the
strength of the relationships we have observed have clear implications for coaches and
practitioners. Whilst overall muscularity appeared important for performance (All muscles:
absolute volume +24% for elite vs sub-elite; performance correlations for absolute [r=-0.629]
and relative [r=-0.422] volume), this belied the fact that there were highly variable and non-
uniform effects for specific muscle groups and muscles. The largest muscle group specific
effects were found primarily for the hip extensors (differences of +32% absolute and +15%
relative volume; explaining 47.5% [absolute volume] to 31.4% [relative volume] of the
variability in performance) and secondarily for the knee flexors (differences of +24% absolute
volume; performance correlations for absolute [r=-0.682] and relative [r=-0.522] volume),
whereas the plantarflexors showed no differences between the sprint groups. This evidence
strongly supports the idea that developing large hip extensors and knee flexors, for example
through resistance training, would be valuable for the sprint athlete looking to enhance
performance (27).
For absolute muscle volumes very similar factors differentiated both sub-elite sprinters from
controls as well as elite vs. sub-elite sprinters (e.g. total muscle volume, four muscle groups in
the same order of magnitude, and five individual muscles; See Table, Supplemental Digital

 vs. controls, and elite sprinters vs. sub-elite sprinters, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C151),
indicating progressive development of these same variables may continuously improve
performance up to elite level. In contrast, for relative volumes, whilst a wide range of factors
distinguished sub-elite sprinters from controls, elite sprinters were differentiated by only four
variables (volume of the hip extensor muscle group, TFL, sartorius and gluteus maximus)
indicating a more targeted development may be needed for elite performance. Moreover, the

                       it may become less critical prior to an important game or event when foods that benefit
                       performance are preferred, particularly in a highly competitive sport. The limited number
                       of studies with athletes has reported performance or competition are one of the most
                       important influences on food choice [8].
                             Our results shown a significant variation in the willingness to taste before and after the
                       information treatment, in line with previous studies [45,49,58,59]. The athlete acceptability
                       of insect-based foods was systematically increased after receiving information about the
                       potential environmental and nutritional benefits of including insects in the diet.
                             Consequently, although recent technological developments in assuring food security
                       for edible insects, e.g., automation and reduction in microbial contamination by person-
                       nel [16,19], the future marketing of these products in professional sport must also ensure
                       that the products do not lead to any anti-doping rule violation.
                             This study has several limitations. First, it is a small sample for a quantitative study,
                       and therefore, we are aware that generalization of the findings is difficult and should be
                       done with caution. However, this is due to the specific target under investigation (profes-
                       sional athletes) which is not allowing to recruit a higher number of respondents. Thus,
                       an extension of the dataset, including the widest variation possible for the sample, may
                       increase the quality of future studies. Moreover, the comparison in nutritional knowledge
                       with other studies was difficult, due to the heterogeneity of the measures used and re-
                       duced number of articles. The questionnaire only measured self-reported willingness to
                       try insects and did not observe actual behavior to eat insects. In fact, in our study, it was
 Foods 2021, 10, 1117                                                                                                             10 of 12




                                  not possible to carry out a “bug experience” that they might be categorized as “hidden
                                  substances” considered as high risk of doping in this specific category of participants. It
                                  is important to identify the species of insect best suited to cover the nutritional needs of
                                  athletes, reducing the risk of doping and optimizing training sessions as well as recovery
                                  and metabolic adaptation.
                                       Future studies should consider using real products (e.g., bars with cricket flour) to
                                  measure actual consumption of insect food [18] and also include the Entomophagy Attitude
                                  Questionnaire Scale [60] instead of the FNS scale, to better investigate the individual
                                  aversion to eating insects.

Tsuyoshi Nagatani1 , Shayne Vial1 , Kristina L. Kendall1                                          , Paul Comfort1,2                     ,
Jiahao Yang1 , and G. Gregory Haff1,2,3


Abstract
It is well documented that cluster sets, a modiﬁed set structure with additional rest between individual repetitions or
groups of repetitions, can be used to modulate exercise-induced fatigue during resistance training. While practical guide-
lines exist, it remains unclear to what extent strength and conditioning (S&C) professionals utilise this programming tac-
tic. The aim of this study was to examine S&C professionals’ perceptions of cluster sets and their application in practice.
A secondary aim was to assess the alignment between cluster set programming tactics used in the ﬁeld and evidence-
based recommendations from the scientiﬁc and coaching literature. Forty-six S&C professionals (age: 40.0 ± 13.6 yrs) com-
pleted an online survey comprised of three sections: (1) coaching demographic, (2) perceptions of cluster sets, and (3) program
design. The survey included both closed- and open-ended questions. There was a general alignment between professional prac-
tice and current recommendations, particularly regarding the use of cluster sets during strength-power phases, manipulation of
rest intervals, and prescription of higher training intensities. However, unlike recommended published practices, cluster sets
were most commonly used with the bench press and variations of the squat, both of which require un-racking and re-racking
the barbell during the cluster set, which may be physically demanding for athletes. Despite acknowledging logistical barriers
such as supervision issues and time constraints, S&C professionals still view cluster sets as a practical programming tactic
due to their minimal technological requirements and potential beneﬁts. These ﬁndings can inform future applied research
projects and educational content focused on cluster sets.

Keywords
Fatigue, inter-repetition rest, intra-set rest, professional practice, resistance training

A secondary aim was to assess the alignment between cluster set programming tactics used in the ﬁeld and evidence-
based recommendations from the scientiﬁc and coaching literature. Forty-six S&C professionals (age: 40.0 ± 13.6 yrs) com-
pleted an online survey comprised of three sections: (1) coaching demographic, (2) perceptions of cluster sets, and (3) program
design. The survey included both closed- and open-ended questions. There was a general alignment between professional prac-
tice and current recommendations, particularly regarding the use of cluster sets during strength-power phases, manipulation of
rest intervals, and prescription of higher training intensities. However, unlike recommended published practices, cluster sets
were most commonly used with the bench press and variations of the squat, both of which require un-racking and re-racking
the barbell during the cluster set, which may be physically demanding for athletes. Despite acknowledging logistical barriers
such as supervision issues and time constraints, S&C professionals still view cluster sets as a practical programming tactic
due to their minimal technological requirements and potential beneﬁts. These ﬁndings can inform future applied research
projects and educational content focused on cluster sets.

{
 "id": "Q22",
 "sourceFile": "The muscle morphology of elite sprint running.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Muscle Morphology of Elite Sprint Running' (Miller et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, published ahead of print 2020) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Track & Field"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A cross-sectional study comparing MRI muscle volumes and isometric strength in 5 elite sprinters (100 m season's best 10.10 s), 26 sub-elite sprinters (10.80 s) and 11 untrained controls, all healthy young men. Total lower-body muscle volume was 48 percent higher in elite and 20 percent higher in sub-elite sprinters than controls. Hip extensor volume (+32 percent absolute vs sub-elite) and gluteus maximus volume (+45 percent) distinguished elite from sub-elite sprinters and were strongly associated with 100 m times, while isometric strength did not differ between the two sprint groups.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The elite group has only five athletes, so its estimates are imprecise. Seven of 26 sub-elite times were estimated from 60 m or 200 m results. Measurements and performance were taken at different times, and the cross-sectional design cannot establish cause.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the hip extensor and gluteus maximus associations as proof that building these muscles will make a sprinter faster, when the study is cross-sectional, in five elite athletes, and shows association only.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Miller R, Balshaw TG, Massey GJ, Maeo S, Lanza MB, Johnston M, et al. The Muscle Morphology of Elite Sprint Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000002522",
  "abstract": "Muscle volumes (MRI) and isometric strength were compared in elite sprinters, sub-elite sprinters and untrained controls, and related to 100 m performance. Total lower-body muscle volume differed across all three groups, hip extensor and gluteus maximus volumes distinguished elite from sub-elite sprinters and tracked sprint times, and isometric strength did not separate the sprint groups.",
  "tldr": "Elite sprinters had larger hip extensor and gluteus maximus volumes than sub-elite sprinters, and these muscles tracked 100 m times. With only five elite athletes and a cross-sectional design, the finding is an association and does not show that building these muscles causes faster sprinting.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional study of 5 elite sprinters, 26 sub-elite sprinters and 11 untrained controls. Muscle volumes were measured from 3T MRI for 23 lower-limb muscles and 5 functional groups, and isometric strength was measured with dynamometers for 5 muscle groups. Groups were compared by one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests. Within the sprint cohort, Pearson correlations (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and stepwise regression related volume and strength to 100 m season's best equivalent.",
  "findings": "Total lower-body volume was controls below sub-elite (+20 percent) below elite (+48 percent). Elite sprinters had greater absolute volume than sub-elite sprinters in four functional groups, with the largest difference in hip extensors (+32 percent absolute, +15 percent relative); plantarflexors did not differ between sprint groups. Gluteus maximus (+45 percent), TFL (+57 percent) and sartorius (+47 percent) were larger in elite sprinters. Across all sprinters, total volume correlated with 100 m time (r = -0.629), and absolute hip extensor volume explained 47.5 percent of the variance. Isometric strength of several groups was greater than controls in both sprint groups, but it did not differ between sprint groups and no strength measure was related to faster sprint times (relative knee extensor strength was related to slower times, r = 0.485).",
  "limitations": "Only five elite sprinters were included, and the authors acknowledge the small elite sample for strength. Seven of 26 sub-elite 100 m times were estimated from 60 m or 200 m results. Strength was tested once without familiarisation, and isometric tests may lack specificity to sprinting. The cross-sectional design cannot show cause, although the authors argue a large causal component is likely.",
  "practicalImplications": "In this sample, hip extensor and gluteus maximus size tracked sprint times, so coaches may track these muscle groups as part of lower-body planning for sprinters. The study does not show that increasing them causes faster sprinting, and isometric strength did not separate the two sprint groups, so it should not be the only marker of elite potential.",
  "athleteDev": "The authors suggest that developing the hip extensors and knee flexors, for example through resistance training, would be valuable for sprinters, and the gluteus maximus findings point to targeted hypertrophy. The evidence is associative and comes from a small sample, so review progress against sprint times rather than assuming a direct effect.",
  "rtp": "The study compares healthy, uninjured men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It should not be used to set rehabilitation loads or muscle-size targets."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.findings: 'not related to sprint time' -> no strength measure related to faster times; relative knee extensor strength related to slower times ('positive relationship between relative knee extensor strength and SBE100 (r= 0.485)'); added plantarflexors showed no sprint-group difference",
   "paper.practicalImplications: 'did not separate the groups' -> 'did not separate the two sprint groups' (strength was greater than controls)",
   "paper.athleteDev: reframed as the authors' own suggestion and added knee flexors ('developing large hip extensors and knee flexors, for example through resistance training, would be valuable')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Text is the published-ahead-of-print manuscript (copyright 2020); final issue year, volume and pages are not printed and may differ.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A questionnaire study of 61 Italian professional athletes (27 women, aged 19 to 39), recruited from one sports centre, that measured supplement use, nutrition knowledge, food neophobia, and willingness to taste and endorse a cricket-flour protein bar before and after an information text. Before the text, 26 athletes were willing to taste, 7 uncertain and 28 unwilling; the authors report a significant increase in willingness after the text (z = 4.16, p < 0.001), and 37.7 percent were willing to endorse the bar.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Small convenience sample from one centre, measured by self-report questionnaire, with no actual tasting or product consumption. The authors acknowledge that the sample limits generalisation and that willingness was not converted into observed behaviour.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the rise in willingness after the information text as proof that athletes will accept insect-based supplements, when the study measured stated intention in one small sample and did not test the product's nutrition, safety or doping risk.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Placentino U, Sogari G, Viscecchia R, De Devitiis B, Monacis L. The New Challenge of Sports Nutrition: Accepting Insect Food as Dietary Supplements in Professional Athletes. Foods. 2021;10:1117.",
  "doi": "10.3390/foods10051117",
  "abstract": "Sixty-one Italian professional athletes completed a questionnaire on supplement use, nutrition knowledge, food neophobia and willingness to taste and endorse a cricket-flour protein bar. Willingness to taste rose after a short information text, and athletes who were willing to taste were more willing to endorse the product.",
  "tldr": "Athletes in this small sample took supplements mainly on the advice of qualified personnel and had weak sports nutrition knowledge. Protein content and curiosity about texture were the main reasons to try an insect bar, while disgust drove refusal.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional questionnaire study of 61 professional athletes recruited on a voluntary basis at the Italian Air Force Sports Centre in Rome. The questionnaire covered supplement use, nutrition knowledge (adapted A-NSKQ), food neophobia (FNS), and willingness to taste and endorse an insect protein bar on a 7-point scale, before and after a short information text. Analysis used descriptive statistics, correlation, regression and repeated-measures tests.",
  "findings": "Every athlete reported using supplements; 88.5 percent named qualified personnel as their main information source. Nutrition knowledge was poor (47.8 percent overall). Before the information text, 26 athletes were willing, 7 uncertain and 28 unwilling to taste the bar; willingness rose after the text (z = 4.16, p < 0.001), particularly among unwilling athletes (z = 3.88, p < 0.001). Forty-three athletes (70.5 percent) were classed as tasters. Only 37.7 percent were willing to endorse the bar, and tasters endorsed it more than non-tasters (4.67 vs 2.22, p < 0.001). Men were more willing to endorse than women (4.47 vs 3.3, p = 0.006). Age was positively associated with food neophobia (r = 0.3, p < 0.05).",
  "limitations": "The sample is small and convenience-based, from one centre and mainly track and field, fencing and beach volleyball athletes. Willingness was self-reported, and no product was tasted, because the authors could not run a tasting session with insects that might count as hidden substances with a high doping risk. The questionnaire used the FNS rather than an insect-specific attitude scale.",

  "athleteDev": "Performance nutrition staff can use these results to frame a novel protein bar around protein content and explain its benefits before asking athletes to try it. The study does not show that the bar supports performance or recovery.",

{
 "id": "Q24",
 "sourceFile": "The perceptions and applications of cluster sets in strength and conditioning.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The perceptions and applications of cluster sets in strength and conditioning' (Nagatani et al., Int J Sports Sci Coach 2025) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "An online survey of 46 strength and conditioning professionals (39 men, 7 women) about how they perceive and programme cluster sets, with closed and open questions analysed by frequency counts and thematic analysis. Thirty-seven (80 percent) reported using cluster sets, most often in the strength-power phase (84 percent of users), and most used percentage of 1RM to set load; the authors judge practice broadly consistent with published recommendations.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample is small, self-selected and recruited through chain sampling, and the survey records coaches' reported perceptions and practice, not athlete training data or outcomes. The authors note that more experienced coaches may differ from those surveyed.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the finding that practice aligns with recommendations as evidence that cluster sets improve athlete performance, when the survey measures what coaches report doing and believing, not athlete results.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Nagatani T, Vial S, Kendall KL, Comfort P, Yang J, Haff GG. The perceptions and applications of cluster sets in strength and conditioning. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025.",
  "doi": "10.1177/17479541251403877",
  "abstract": "Forty-six strength and conditioning professionals completed an online survey on their perceptions of cluster sets and how they programme them. The authors report general alignment with published recommendations, except that cluster sets were most often used with bench press and squat variants, which require un-racking and re-racking the bar and may be physically demanding.",
  "tldr": "Most coaches surveyed use cluster sets, mainly in strength-power phases, and they report raising intensity by about 2 to 15 percent of 1RM for cluster sets. Logistics such as supervising large groups and added training time are the main barriers.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional online survey of 46 strength and conditioning professionals, recruited by email, social media and chain sampling. Closed-ended questions were analysed by frequency counts, and open-ended responses were analysed by six-stage thematic analysis.",
  "findings": "37 of 46 respondents (80 percent) used cluster sets. Strength-power phase use was reported by 31 of 37 users (84 percent), compared with 13 (35 percent) for hypertrophy or strength-endurance. Percentage of 1RM was the most common load method (23 of 37, 62 percent). Bench press and squat variants were the most common exercises. Nineteen of 37 users (51 percent) reported no concerns; the most common concerns were extended training duration (27 percent) and supervision of large groups (24 percent).",
  "limitations": "Perceptions and self-reported practice only, with no athlete data. Small, self-selected sample recruited through chain sampling. The authors note that the questionnaire did not capture whether the programmes used were evidence based or the athletes' training histories.",
  "practicalImplications": "Cluster sets are most often used in strength-power blocks with intensity raised by about 2 to 15 percent of 1RM, so programmes that use them should plan the added rest and supervision needed for the session. The survey cannot show whether those choices improve performance, so test them on your own athletes before relying on them.",
  "athleteDev": "Coaches can use these survey patterns to plan cluster sets in strength-power phases with a load increase and longer rest, and to check that the session time and supervision are realistic for the group. The paper does not show performance gains from these choices.",
  "rtp": "The study does not address rehabilitation or return to sport and should not be used to set return-to-sport loads."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.tldr/practicalImplications: load increase 'about 5 to 15 percent' -> '2 to 15 percent of 1RM' ('practitioners increase training intensity by 2-15% of 1RM')",
   "paper.abstract: 'heavy bench press and squat variants' -> bench press and squat variants needing un-racking and re-racking (no 'heavy' in text)",
   "paper.limitations: removed stray punctuation"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}
